findings.title: Google credential is saved as the zod SafeParse result object instead of the key
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the safeParse result (`{ success, data }`), not the parsed data. The old code was `const key = googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)`, which returned the plain key. Now `key` is `{ success: true, data: {...} }` and is written to `credential.key` via `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. After the first token refresh every Google Calendar credential is corrupted. The next `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` in `googleAuth` fails, so Google Calendar breaks for any user whose token refreshes. The fix is to pass `key.data` (or unwrap the result) when saving.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses computed keys that evaluate to "[object Object]", so expiry and other fields are stripped
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` are computed property keys. A zod type has no custom `toString`, so both evaluate to the literal string `"[object Object]"`. The second entry overwrites the first, so the schema is effectively `{ access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown? }`. `z.object` strips unknown keys by default. In credential-sync mode the parsed data therefore contains only `access_token`: `expires_in`, `expiry_date`, `scope`, `token_type` and the rest are dropped. Callers such as Zoom (`newTokens.expires_in`) then compute `Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)`, which is `NaN`, and store a broken `expiry_date`. Salesforce loses `instance_url` the same way. The comment says "any property with a number is the expiry", but this does not implement that. Use `.passthrough()` or `.catchall(z.unknown())`, and define the expiry field explicitly.

findings.title: Placeholder refresh_token is injected in every mode and can overwrite a real refresh token
findings.body: `if (!data.refresh_token) data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` runs for the normal (non-sync) path too, not only in credential-sync mode. For the Office 365 calendar flow, `refresh_token` is optional in `refreshTokenResponseSchema`. If Microsoft omits it from the refresh response, the merge `{...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data}` replaces the user's real refresh token with the string `"refresh_token"`. Every later refresh then fails and the credential is permanently broken. In sync mode the placeholder also overwrites the stored token in Zoom (`key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token`). The placeholder should only be applied in sync mode, and it should never overwrite an existing value.

findings.title: `prisma` is used but never imported in the Salesforce CalendarService
findings.body: The new refresh block calls `prisma.credential.update(...)`, but the file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a TypeScript error and a runtime `ReferenceError`. `getClient` runs in the constructor, so every Salesforce calendar operation fails.

findings.title: Salesforce refresh is unconditional, bypasses refreshOAuthTokens, and the new token is not used
findings.body: `getClient` now calls `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` on every instantiation, whether or not the token is expired. That adds a network call and a DB write per use, and risks rate limiting. It does not go through `refreshOAuthTokens`, so credential sync is never used for Salesforce and the self-hoster's endpoint is ignored. The `jsforce.Connection` is still built with the old `credentialKey.access_token` rather than the freshly fetched one. `response.statusText !== "OK"` is unreliable because HTTP/2 responses have an empty `statusText`, so it would throw 400 even on success. In sync mode the stripped schema also drops `instance_url` from the stored key.

findings.title: credentialId is passed where refreshOAuthTokens expects the Cal.com userId
findings.body: `refreshAccessToken(credentialId, credentialKey)` only has the credential id, and that value is passed as the third argument (`userId`) of `refreshOAuthTokens`. In sync mode the POST sends `calcomUserId=<credentialId>`, so the self-hoster's endpoint returns tokens for the wrong user, or none. When `userId` happens to be falsy the sync is silently skipped. The credential's `userId` must be threaded through to this method.

findings.title: Sync mode returns a raw fetch Response, but several callers expect their SDK/axios result shape
findings.body: In sync mode `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` `Response`. In non-sync mode it returns whatever each caller's `refreshFunction` returns. Several callers rely on the latter shape and break in sync mode. Google reads `res?.data`, Zoho CRM and Zoho Bigin read `tokenInfo.data` (axios shape), and HubSpot expects a token object with `expiresIn` and `accessToken`. With a `Response` these are all `undefined`: Google throws `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'access_token')`, and the Zoho and HubSpot flows fail or log errors. The helper needs to normalise the response (check `response.ok`, parse the JSON, and wrap it to match each caller's expected shape). The unauthenticated POST also has no error handling for non-2xx responses.

findings.title: Webex still validates the refresh response with the strict schema, so sync mode always fails
findings.body: Webex was wired to `refreshOAuthTokens` but not to `parseRefreshTokenResponse`. The synced response is documented as containing only the access token and expiry. `webexRefreshedTokenSchema` requires `scope`, `token_type`, `refresh_token` and `refresh_token_expires_in`, so `safeParse` fails and the code rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". Credential sync therefore cannot work for Webex.

findings.title: Behavior change: a bad refresh response now throws, and the diagnostic log was dropped
findings.body: Previously a failed `safeParse` was tolerated: the code logged the zod error and the MS response, then continued with the existing credentials. `parseRefreshTokenResponse` now throws a generic "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned", and the `console.error` with the zod error and MS response was removed. Failures are harder to debug, and the leftover `tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data` check is now dead code. This change in error semantics for non-sync users is not mentioned in the PR.

findings.title: Unhandled exceptions from body validation, decryption and JSON parsing produce 500s
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a ZodError on a malformed body, so the caller gets an opaque 500 instead of a 400. `symmetricDecrypt(...)` and `JSON.parse(...)` at lines 57-59 can also throw if the key is wrong or the payload is not valid JSON. Use `safeParse` and try/catch around decrypt and parse, and return 400 with a clear message. Otherwise self-hosters cannot tell a bad payload from a server fault, and a bad or missing `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` shows up only as a 500.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time `!==`
findings.body: This endpoint writes arbitrary OAuth credentials for any user and is protected only by a shared secret. The secret is compared with `!==`, which is not timing-safe. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. There is also no method check (any HTTP verb is accepted) and no rate limiting.

findings.title: No tests for the new credential webhook or the refresh/sync logic
findings.body: The PR adds a credential-writing webhook and changes token refresh in about ten apps, but ships no tests. The PR checklist says tests were not added. The bugs found above (corrupted Google key, stripped schema fields, wrong user id) would have been caught by basic unit tests of `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, `refreshOAuthTokens` and the webhook handler.
